 How Did ‘The Day After Tomorrow’ Become the Top Movie on Netflix in 2026? 
 By Jesse Hassenger 
 Published 
 Nov. 3, 2026, 9:15 a.m. ET

 Way back in 2004, it was still possible for a movie to make $150 million or more at the U.S. box office mostly based on what kind of movie it looked like, rather than how well it actually turned out. There are examples of this quality from throughout film history, but 2004 seems like a particularly potent year for it, given the success of movies like Shark Tale (looks like a more farcical Finding Nemo ; is actually one of the most hideous big-studio cartoons ever made); I, Robot (looks like a slick Will Smith sci-fi thriller with a serious-author pedigree; is actually almost incalculably stupid); Troy (looks like an old-fashioned historical epic; still gets mistaken for one, mostly because it was shot on 35mm and stars Brad Pitt); and The Grudge (looks like The Ring ; just plain isn’t), among others. You could even argue that the year’s biggest movie, Shrek 2 , was essentially its own Shrek lookalike. 
 But there may be no better instance of 2004 Lookalike Cinema than The Day After Tomorrow , a movie that looks so much like a certain kind of movie that it can still jump to the top of the Netflix charts more than 22 years after its release.
 The Day After Tomorrow was a designated return to form for director Roland Emmerich, who became known as a master of disaster with movies like Independence Day and, to a lesser extent, the 1998 Godzilla (both made with his longtime collaborator Dean Devlin). Following Godzilla ‘s underperformance and the success of the 2000 war drama The Patriot , Emmerich returned to the disaster genre sans Devlin with The Day After Tomorrow . Just as Independence Day was sold on the indelible image of the White House getting blown to smithereens, The Day After Tomorrow was sold on a killer poster image: New York City, buried in hundreds of feet of snow, even covering the Statue of Liberty.
 Photo: Everett Collection 
 The perpetrator this time was not alien invaders, but climate change, giving the movie a contemporary kick where Emmerich’s previous disaster movies threw back to the 1970s heyday of the genre. The movie also had a more focused cast than the Independence Day ensemble, with scientist Dennis Quaid attempting to rescue his storm-stranded son played by Jake Gyllenhaal; a young Emmy Rossum is there, too. This all helps differentiate the movie from Emmerich’s other work while maintaining his work’s baseline watach-ability.
 At the same time, The Day After Tomorrow doesn’t have a star performance as commanding as Will Smith’s. It also doesn’t have a speech as rousing as Bill Pullman’s. Nor does that icy New York City really hold a candle to the visceral thrill of all of those decimated landmarks (including, hey, the Statue of Liberty!) from Emmerich’s previous hit. No wonder, then, that after a mega opening weekend, The Day After Tomorrow played like plenty of other summer blockbusters, doing a fast fade in the U.S., while grossing a very strong $550 million-plus globally. (Big disaster imagery always travels well.) It definitely did better numbers than the Emmerich Godzilla . At the same time… maybe not that much better. Adjusting for 19980-to-2004 inflation, it made about $25 million more in the U.S. The jump up in other countries was more, but then, international markets for U.S. movies in general expanded in the 2000s. Yet 22 years later, The Day After Tomorrow has enough A-list juice to top the Netflix charts, while the 1998 Godzilla is more of a Tubi attraction. (It rotates between the free-with-ads services pretty steadily.) 
 Photo: Everett Collection 
 Maybe that’s just the enduring sexiness of Jake Gyllenhaal triumphing over a nerdy Matthew Broderick, or the Emmy Rossum bump after Furious . But there’s something about The Day After Tomorrow that feels like a turning point in the disaster movie subgenre. The film’s success inspired plenty more apocalyptic and/or extreme-weather narratives, including Emmerich’s own 2012 and his collaborator Dean Devlin’s Geostorm . 2012 , at least, was a sizable hit. But returns were diminishing; it made a little bit less than Day After Tomorrow , five years later, inching further away from those Independence Day heights and back to Godzilla territory. Global-disaster blowouts had peaked in the 20th century, and in retrospect The Day After Tomorrow was more like an echo boom from the ’90s. 
 Now, this shift can’t have been an entirely and immediate post-9/11 pivot from finding entertainment in large-scale destruction; big-screen annihilation on that scale never really went anywhere post-9/11, though it sometimes took on a different tone. (See Spielberg’s War of the Worlds , very much a post-9/11 version of Independence Day that is genuinely harrowing instead of pure popcorn fun.) It’s also hard to argue that we as a country truly sobered up about mankind’s effects on climate change in the 2000s, even though it would have made sense to do that. The effect may have been more subconscious: As visual effects technology improved, it became easier to stage massive, world-ending disasters — and also easier to ignore them. Compared to the scorched Earth of Independence Day , The Day After Tomorrow actually feels a little pedestrian. 2012 is bigger and cartoonier, but that gives it an unreal, screensaver quality that eliminates any real sense of gravity. It also lacks the comforting, almost homespun corniness of a scene where arctic cold chases characters around a hallway. (There are also wolves.)
 ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection 
 That elimination of more believable elements (or at least, less planetary-scale implausibilities) was probably necessary to get a post-9/11 audience, increasingly experiencing the actual effects of terrible storms and weather phenomena, engaged in disaster movies as silly fun. But it also served to make disaster movies look more otherworldly, like any other big-screen fantasy, and less like a fusion of real-life weight and Hollywood magic.
 Given all that, there’s something weirdly nostalgic about The Day After Tomorrow in 2026. It may have been “Lookalike Cinema,” but it also feels, in retrospect, like the last disaster movie where lookalike status was enough to get by — the last one that managed to fake its way toward event status. (It was the biggest non-sequel of its summer!) It had the last shred of plausibility as an environmental message movie buried under all that disaster-picture CGI. Since then, the disasters have been far too close at hand to enjoy the increasing fakery.
